God's parental love and Israel's rebellion (verses 1–7)

God loved the Israelites while they were weak, helpless, foolish and stubborn like little children.

He carried and fed them as a nurse cares for an infant, enduring their difficult behavior.

Everyone who has grown up should often remember God's kindness during childhood.

The Lord cared for us and worked patiently with us, not only like a father or teacher, but like a mother or nurse.

In the wilderness, he showed Israel the way forward and held them by the arms.

Through the ceremonial law given to Moses, he instructed them in his commandments.

He guided them to keep them from wandering and supported them to keep them from falling.

In the same way God's spiritual Israel depends upon his sustaining power.

It is God who draws souls to himself.

No one can come to him unless he draws that person.

He bound the people with cords of love, described by a word Henry understands as stronger than the earlier cords.

He relieved the heavy burdens they had endured.

Yet Israel responded with terrible ingratitude.

God's counsel would have saved them, but their own plans brought ruin.

They repeatedly turned away.

They could not be relied upon to remain faithful.

They turned from God, the highest good, and eagerly embraced temptation.

Their hearts had become set on doing evil.

True happiness belongs only to people whom God teaches by his Spirit, sustains by his power, and leads in his ways.

Through grace he removes the desire and dominion of sin, creates a longing for the gospel's blessed feast, and enables people to feed upon it and live forever.

God's mercy remains available (verses 8–12)

God is slow to anger and unwilling to abandon completely the people called by his name.

When a sacrifice was needed for sin and a Savior for sinners, he did not spare his own Son, so that he might spare us.

Such mercy is offered during the day of God's patience.

People who persist in sin until they exhaust that opportunity will face the great day of his wrath.

Human compassion is small compared with God's tender mercy.

His ways of welcoming returning sinners are as far above ours as heaven is above earth.

God knows how to forgive miserable sinners.

He is faithful and just to forgive because Christ has purchased pardon, and God himself has promised it.

Our trembling at Christ's word should draw us toward him, not drive us away.

The children who tremble should run to their Father.

Everyone responding to the gospel invitation will receive a place and a name in the gospel church.

Israel's religious service had become hypocritical.

In Judah, however, the people still showed regard for God's law and followed their faithful ancestors.

Let us remain faithful.

God honors those who honor him, while those who despise him will be lightly regarded.
classic_reading:
[Hos.11.1-Hos.11.7]
Chapter 11
God's regard for Israel; their ingratitude. (Hos. 11:1-7) The Divine mercy yet in store. (Hos. 11:8-12)
Verses 1-7 When Israel were weak and helpless as children, foolish and froward as children, then God loved them; he bore them as the nurse does the sucking child, nourished them, and suffered their manners. All who are grown up, ought often to reflect upon the goodness of God to them in their childhood. He took care of them, took pains with them, not only as a father, or a tutor, but as a mother, or nurse. When they were in the wilderness, God showed them the way in which they should go, and bore them up, taking them by the arms. He taught them the way of his commandments by the ceremonial law given by Moses. He took them by the arms, to guide them, that they might not stray, and to hold them up, that they might not stumble and fall. God's spiritual Israel are all thus supported. It is God's work to draw poor souls to himself; and none can come to him except he draw them. With bands of love; this word signifies stronger cords than the former. He eased them of the burdens they had long groaned under. Israel is very ungrateful to God. God's counsels would have saved them, but their own counsels ruined them. They backslide; there is no hold of them, no stedfastness in them. They backslide from me, from God, the chief good. They are bent to backslide; they are ready to sin; they are forward to close with every temptation. Their hearts are fully set in them to do evil. Those only are truly happy, whom the Lord teaches by his Spirit, upholds by his power, and causes to walk in his ways. By his grace he takes away the love and dominion of sin, and creates a desire for the blessed feast of the gospel, that they may feed thereon, and live for ever.
[Hos.11.8-Hos.11.12]
Verses 8-12 God is slow to anger, and is loth to abandon a people to utter ruin, who have been called by his name. When God was to give a sacrifice for sin, and a Saviour for sinners, he spared not his own Son, that he might spare us. This is the language of the day of his patience; but when men sin that away, then the great day of his wrath comes. Man's compassions are nothing in comparison with the tender mercies of our God, whose thoughts and ways, in receiving returning sinners, are as much above ours as heaven is above the earth. God knows how to pardon poor sinners. He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and therein declares his righteousness, now Christ has purchased the pardon, and he has promised it. Holy trembling at the word of Christ will draw us to him, not drive us from him, the children tremble, and flee to him. And all that come at the gospel call, shall have a place and a name in the gospel church. The religious service of Israel were mere hypocrisy, but in Judah regard was had to God's laws, and the people followed their pious forefathers. Let us be faithful: those who thus honour God, he will honour, but such us despise Him shall be lightly esteemed.

Remember Jacob and return to the Lord (verses 1–6)

Ephraim nourished false hopes of receiving human help while living in hostility toward God.

The Jews imagined they could secure Egypt's support by offering gifts from the produce of their land.

Judah, too, was called to account.

God sees the sins of his own people and will judge them.

Israel was reminded both of what Jacob did and of what God did for Jacob.

When Jacob's faith in God's promise overcame his fears, he prevailed through God's strength in prayer.

God is Jehovah, the same yesterday, today and forever.

What was once a revelation to an individual is now a lasting memorial of God for all generations.

Those who have departed from God should return to him through repentance and faith, acknowledging him as their God.

Those already converted should walk faithfully with him in holy conduct.

Let us wrestle in prayer for the blessings he has promised, determined to continue seeking him rather than give up.

Let us seek him in the ordinances of his worship.

Israel's dishonest prosperity (verses 7–14)

Ephraim became a merchant.

Henry notes that the word can also mean a Canaanite.

The people traded on Canaanite principles, pursuing profit through greed, fraud and deceit.

They became wealthy and imagined that their prosperity proved God's favor.

But shameful sins bring shameful judgments.

They should remember not only Jacob's power with God, but also the years he served Laban.

When God has given us the privilege of his word, disregarding it makes our sin and folly all the more serious.

It is better to labor under the hardest conditions in honest poverty than to gain riches through sin.

We should compare our conduct with that of faithful believers who faced similar circumstances in the past.

Those who despise God's message will perish.

May we all receive his word with humble and obedient faith.

[Hos.12.1-Hos.12.6]
Chapter 12
Judah and Israel reminded of the Divine favours. (Hos. 12:1-6) The provocations of Israel. (Hos. 12:7-14)
Verses 1-6 Ephraim feeds himself with vain hopes of help from man, when he is at enmity with God. The Jews vainly thought to secure the Egyptians by a present of the produce of their country. Judah is contended with also. God sees the sin of his own people, and will reckon with them for it. They are put in mind of what Jacob did, and what God did for him. When his faith upon the Divine promise prevailed above his fears, then by his strength he had power with God. He is Jehovah, the same that was, and is, and is to come. What was a revelation of God to one, is his memorial to many, to all generations. Then let those who have gone from God, be turned to him. Turn thou to the Lord, by repentance and faith, as thy God. Let those that are converted to him, walk with him in all holy conversation and godliness. Let us wrestle with Him for promised blessings, determined not to give over till we prevail; and let us seek Him in his ordinances.
[Hos.12.7-Hos.12.14]
Verses 7-14 Ephraim became a merchant: the word also signifies a Canaanite. They carried on trade upon Canaanitish principles, covetously and with fraud and deceit. Thus they became rich, and falsely supposed that Providence favoured them. But shameful sins shall have shameful punishments. Let them remember, not only what a mighty prince Jacob was with God, but what a servant he was to Laban. The benefits we have had from the word of God, make our sin and folly the worse, if we put any slight upon that word. We had better follow the hardest labour in poverty, than grow rich by sin. We may form a judgment of our own conduct, by comparing it with that of ancient believers in the like circumstances. Whoever despises the message of God, will perish. May we all hear his word with humble, obedient faith.

Ephraim turns from God to idols (verses 1–8)

As long as Ephraim reverenced and worshiped God, the tribe held an honored place.

But when Ephraim abandoned God for idols, it fell from that position.

The people who sacrificed to idols were told to kiss the calves, expressing worship, affection and submission.

But the Lord will not give his glory to another.

Those who worship images will therefore be brought to shame.

No lasting and genuine comfort is found anywhere except in God.

The Lord not only cared for Israel during the wilderness years; he also brought the people into Canaan, a fertile and pleasant land.

Yet worldly success, when it feeds pride, makes people forget God.

Therefore the Lord would confront them in judgment like the fiercest beasts of their forests.

Abusing divine goodness leads to more severe judgment.

Destruction through sin and mercy through redemption (verses 9–16)

Israel had destroyed itself through rebellion.

It could not rescue itself.

Its only help came from the Lord.

The same truth applies to spiritual redemption from the lost condition into which all human beings have fallen through deliberate sins.

God sometimes gives sinners the very things they wrongfully demand, but in displeasure.

For faithful believers, whether God gives or takes away, he acts in love.

For the unrepentant, both receiving and losing earthly things can become expressions of wrath and bring no true comfort.

Without repentance and faith in the gospel, sinners will soon face severe distress.

Israel's predicted national ruin also contained the promise that God would intervene mercifully and powerfully to preserve a remnant.

Yet that deliverance only foreshadowed the redemption of the true Israel through Christ's death, burial and resurrection.

Christ will destroy death and the grave.

The Lord will not abandon his promise or change his purpose.

In the meantime, Israel would be devastated for its sins.

Without good works bearing fruit through the Holy Spirit, other kinds of prosperity are as empty as uncertain worldly wealth.

God's judgment would dry up the branches and wither the shoots.

Those who rebel against him would face suffering worse than even the cruelty of warfare.

May the Lord save us from such misery and from sin, its cause.

[Hos.13.1-Hos.13.8]
Chapter 13
The abuse of God's favour leads to punishment. (Hos. 13:1-8) A promise of God's mercy. (Hos. 13:9-16)
Verses 1-8 While Ephraim kept up a holy fear of God, and worshipped Him in that fear, so long he was very considerable. When Ephraim forsook God, and followed idolatry, he sunk. Let the men that sacrifice kiss the calves, in token of their adoration of them, affection for them, and obedience to them; but the Lord will not give his glory to another, and therefore all that worship images shall be confounded. No solid, lasting comfort, is to be expected any where but in God. God not only took care of the Israelites in the wilderness, he put them in possession of Canaan, a good land; but worldly prosperity, when it feeds men's pride, makes them forgetful of God. Therefore the Lord would meet them in just vengeance, as the most terrible beast that inhabited their forests. Abused goodness calls for greater severity.
[Hos.13.9-Hos.13.16]
Verses 9-16 Israel had destroyed himself by his rebellion; but he could not save himself, his help was from the Lord only. This may well be applied to the case of spiritual redemption, from that lost state into which all have fallen by wilful sins. God often gives in displeasure what we sinfully desire. It is the happiness of the saints, that, whether God gives or takes away, all is in love. But it is the misery of the wicked, that, whether God gives or takes away, it is all in wrath, nothing is comfortable. Except sinners repent and believe the gospel, anguish will soon come upon them. The prophecy of the ruin of Israel as a nation, also showed there would be a merciful and powerful interposition of God, to save a remnant of them. Yet this was but a shadow of the ransom of the true Israel, by the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ. He will destroy death and the grave. The Lord would not repent of his purpose and promise. Yet, in the mean time, Israel would be desolated for her sins. Without fruitfulness in good works, springing from the Holy Spirit, all other fruitfulness will be found as empty as the uncertain riches of the world. The wrath of God will wither its branches, its sprigs shall be dried up, it shall come to nothing. Woes, more terrible than any from the most cruel warfare, shall fall on those who rebel against God. From such miseries, and from sin, the cause of them, may the Lord deliver us.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesAn exhortation to repentance.1–3Blessings promised, showing the rich comforts of the gospel.4–8The just and the wicked.9
Return to the Lord with words of repentance (verses 1–3)

Israel was urged to turn from sins and idols and return to Jehovah.

The people were to come through faith in God's mercy and grace through the promised Redeemer and through careful attention to worship and service.

Take away our wrongdoing, they prayed.

Remove it as a heavy burden under which we are sinking, or as a stumbling block over which we repeatedly fall.

Take all of it away through a free and complete pardon, because we cannot remove it ourselves.

Receive our prayer graciously.

The people did not prescribe exactly which earthly benefit they desired.

They entrusted the outcome to God.

What they needed was not the good the world could show, but the good God could give.

They had to consider their sins, their needs and the remedy.

Instead of bringing sacrifices as the substance of repentance, they were to bring words that expressed their hearts' true desires.

This clearly portrays a sinner's conversion to God through Jesus Christ.

When approaching God in prayer and faith, we should first ask him to teach us what to pray for.

We must earnestly plead that he remove all our sins.

God promises healing, love and fruitfulness (verses 4–8)

Israel was invited to seek God's favor and would not seek it in vain.

He would turn away his anger.

When God loves, he loves freely.

His love does not arise from people's merit but from his own gracious pleasure.

God will be for his people everything they need.

The gifts of his Spirit are like hidden manna or dew.

Grace freely given will not be wasted.

His people will grow upward, becoming beautiful like a lily (Matthew 6:28–29).

They will also grow downward, becoming deeply rooted like the cedars of Lebanon.

Much of genuine spiritual growth occurs in the hidden roots, where it is unseen.

They will also spread like a vine, with branches reaching outward.

When believers abound in good works, their branches extend and help others.

They will be pleasing both to God and to other people.

Holiness is the soul's beauty.

The church resembles a vine and an olive tree that bear useful fruit.

God's promises belong to people who remain under the care of his appointed ordinances, not those who flee briefly into their shade merely to escape a passing hardship.

When a person comes to God, others dwelling under that person's influence benefit too.

The fruits of holiness will become visible in life.

Thus believers grow in the experience and fruitfulness of the gospel.

Ephraim will say, “What have I to do with idols anymore?”

God himself puts that resolve into the person's heart.

God's promises are a stronger foundation for putting sin to death than our promises to him.

Divine grace changes the heart so deeply that former idols become as hateful as they once were beloved.

Even suffering can be sanctified for that purpose.

Ephraim suffered because of idolatry, and the intended fruit was the removal of sin (Isaiah 27:9).

True repentance means a firm determination to have nothing more to do with sin.

The Lord receives repentant people mercifully, as the father welcomed his returning prodigal son.

God becomes their delight and defense.

They can rest happily in his shade.

The Lord himself supplies the root from which all good fruit grows.

From him come the grace and strength needed for duty.

The righteous walk in God's ways (verse 9)

Who benefits from the prophet's teaching?

Those who earnestly try to understand and know these truths.

God's providential ways are right: he does everything well.

Christ is a foundation stone to some.

To others, he becomes a stumbling stone and rock of offense.

Something appointed to bring life can, when abused through unbelief, lead instead to death.

The same sun softens wax and hardens clay.

Those who turn away even while walking among God's ordinances are in great danger.

They stumble over the Rock of Ages and draw poison from the Balm of Gilead.

Let sinners in Zion take warning.

May we learn to walk in the Lord's right ways as faithful servants, and may none of us stumble at his word through disobedience and unbelief.
classic_reading:
[Hos.14.1-Hos.14.3]
Chapter 14
An exhortation to repentance. (Hos. 14:1-3) Blessings promised, showing the rich comforts of the gospel. (Hos. 14:4-8) The just and the wicked. (Hos. 14:9)
Verses 1-3 Israel is exhorted to return unto Jehovah, from their sins and idols, by faith in his mercy, and grace through the promised Redeemer, and by diligently attending on his worship and service. Take away iniquity; lift it off as a burden we are ready to sink under, or as the stumbling-block we have often fallen over. Take it all away by a free and full forgiveness, for we cannot strike any of it off. Receive our prayer graciously. They do not say what good they seek, but refer it to God. It is not good of the world's showing, but good of God's giving. They were to consider their sins, their wants, and the remedy; and they were to take, not sacrifices, but words stating the desires of their hearts, and with them to address the Lord. The whole forms a clear description of the nature and tendency of a sinner's conversion to God through Jesus Christ. As we draw near to God by the prayer of faith, we should first beseech him to teach us what to ask. We must be earnest with him to take away all iniquity.
[Hos.14.4-Hos.14.8]
Verses 4-8 Israel seeks God's face, and they shall not seek it in vain. His anger is turned from them. Whom God loves, he loves freely; not because they deserve it, but of his own good pleasure. God will be to them all they need. The graces of the Spirit are the hidden manna, hidden in the dew; the grace thus freely bestowed on them shall not be in vain. They shall grow upward, and be more flourishing; shall grow as the lily. The lily, when come to its height, is a lovely flower, Matt. 6:28,29. They shall grow downward, and be more firm. With the flower of the lily shall be the strong root of the cedar of Lebanon. Spiritual growth consists most in the growth of the root, which is out of sight. They shall also spread as the vine, whose branches extend very widely. When believers abound in good works, then their branches spread. They shall be acceptable both to God and man. Holiness is the beauty of a soul. The church is compared to the vine and the olive, which bring forth useful fruits. God's promises pertain to those only that attend on his ordinances; not such as flee to this shadow only for shelter in a hot gleam, but all who dwell under it. When a man is brought to God, all who dwell under his shadow fare the better. The sanctifying fruits shall appear in his life. Thus believers grow up into the experience and fruitfulness of the gospel. Ephraim shall say, God will put it into his heart to say it, What have I to do any more with idols! God's promises to us are more our security and our strength for mortifying sin, than our promises to God. See the power of Divine grace. God will work such a change in him, that he shall loathe the idols as much as ever he loved them. See the benefit of sanctified afflictions. Ephraim smarted for his idolatry, and this is the fruit, even the taking away his sin, [Isa.27.9] Is. 27:9. See the nature of repentance; it is a firm and fixed resolution to have no more to do with sin. The Lord meets penitents with mercy, as the father of the prodigal met his returning son. God will be to all true converts both a delight and a defence; they shall sit under his shadow with delight. And as the root of a tree; From me is thy fruit found: from Him we receive grace and strength to enable us to do our duty.
[Hos.14.9]
Verse 9 Who profit by the truths the prophet delivered? Such as set themselves to understand and know these things. The ways of God's providence towards us are right; all is well done. Christ is a Foundation Stone to some, to others a Stone of stumbling, and a Rock of offence. That which was ordained to life, becomes, through their abuse of it, death to them. The same sun softens wax and hardens clay. But those transgressors certainly have the most dangerous, fatal falls, who fall in the ways of God, who split on the Rock of Ages, and suck poison out of the Balm of Gilead. Let sinners in Zion fear this. May we learn to walk in the right ways of God, as his righteous servants, and may none of us be disobedient and unbelieving, and stumble at the word.
